sections.html:
Hillsboro is the seat of Washington County, which lies about 20 miles west of Portland and ranks second in Oregon by population (611,708 in the 2025 estimate). The Portland Metro urban growth boundary slices through it, leaving suburban neighborhoods on one side and farmland on the other. Beaverton, Tigard, Sherwood, Forest Grove, Cornelius, Banks, Gaston and North Plains are among the other cities.

Intel and Nike anchor the job market, which makes commute questions common.

Valuation and collection both belong to the Department of Assessment and Taxation, found at 155 N. First Avenue, Suite 130, in Hillsboro. Because appraisal, recording and payment share one office, a sale is easy to coordinate.

Walk-in service is weekdays, 8:30 a.m. until 5 p.m. A rear drop box never closes. Phone ahead around holidays.

One tax dollar divides as follows, with schools getting the largest share:

  • Education: 47.38 cents
  • Cities and special districts: 32.42 cents
  • Washington County: 16.82 cents
  • Regional governments: 3.38 cents

Permanent rates date to 1995 and are set at $5 per $1,000 of real market value for schools and $10 per $1,000 for general government. Voters can add bonds and local option levies on top. Hillsboro has a police, fire and parks levy, for instance, and Beaverton has a school levy for teachers. Levies vary by district, so identical houses can carry unequal bills.

The bill starts from assessed value, meaning whichever is smaller: real market value (RMV) or maximum assessed value (MAV). The assessor sets RMV as the likely sale price on January 1, and RMV itself has no cap.

MAV grows at most 3% annually. Even so, a bill can jump further when a district passes a new bond or local option levy, or when major renovations were finished before January 1.

The county mails statements by October 25 and expects payment November 15. You can pay everything or take thirds, and full payment that is postmarked or received by the deadline earns 3% off.

  • Online or by phone (a convenience fee applies to ACH and cards).
  • By mail to 155 N. 1st Avenue, Suite 130, MS 8, Hillsboro, OR 97124. Never mail cash, and do not staple a check to the stub.
  • At the counter or the drop box at the Public Services Building.

The color of the statement tells you who is paying. Green means the owner handles the bill. Yellow means a mortgage company or the Oregon Department of Revenue requested it, so after a purchase, sale or refinance, check with the lender that payment will continue. Past-due money shows on the statement and goes to the oldest year first. An asterisk beside a year marks foreclosure proceedings.

Disagree with the value? File a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board, which used to be named the Board of Property Tax Appeals. Petitions are accepted from the day statements go in the mail through December 31. Washington County asks for no fee, and a lawyer is optional.

  • Only the current year’s value is on the table, never the amount of tax.
  • Hearings are held from the first Monday in February to April 15; showing up is your choice.
  • Bring a recent sale, a fee appraisal or comparable homes near January 1.
  • Still unhappy after the ruling? The Magistrate Division of the Oregon Tax Court hears the next round. Filing costs $50 and must happen within 30 days of the board’s order.

Questions go to 503-846-3854. Your case should rest on what the house was worth on January 1 of the tax year.

The county levies a transfer tax on sales: one dollar for every thousand of the price. Buyer and seller share the liability.

Pay it, or file a claim for exemption, within 15 days after the deed is recorded. Waiting longer triggers a penalty. The county publishes exemption forms for these cases:

  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and court-ordered transfers
  • Trustee’s deeds from foreclosure
  • Gifts, devises and inheritances
  • Transfers between spouses under a dissolution or separation order
  • Sales under $13,999

The Recording Division at the Hillsboro address processes these. A house you inherited is treated differently from a plain sale, so your title company should tell you which form to file.

Escrow does the arithmetic, and the answer turns on when you close. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. If you close between July 1 and mid-October, the buyer will owe the coming bill, so you give the buyer a credit for your share, figured from last year’s tax.

If you close between mid-October and June 30, the bill has typically been paid by you already, and the buyer repays you for the stretch after the agreed transfer date. Escrow also requests payoff figures for liens. Money liens are usually settled from the proceeds, which leaves the buyer with clear title.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes or a deferral lien owed
sections.html:
Back taxes and deferral liens are paid out of the proceeds or cleared before closing, so learn the balance early. Two state programs, the Senior Citizen’s Deferral (age 62 or older) and the Disabled Citizen’s Deferral, let the Department of Revenue pay your tax in exchange for a lien and 6% interest. That money comes due later. A deferred account is flagged at the bottom of the statement.

Tax foreclosure moves slowly but it does happen. ORS 312.010 lets the county foreclose after three years of delinquency, counted from the earliest unpaid year. ORS 312.120 gives owners two more years after judgment to redeem. The county may keep, transfer or auction what it takes. If you are behind, a sale before judgment leaves the house with you.

sections.h2: Before you list: a quick checklist
sections.html: Start with your latest statement: note its color, the balance, and any asterisk on an earlier year. If the figures look off, call the payment line. Ask the appeals line whether a value petition makes sense before December 31. Then tell your title company about any deferral or inheritance so the right transfer tax form is ready, and give the escrow officer a recent statement so the proration is correct.

faqs.q: When are Washington County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The main due date is November 15. Statements are mailed by October 25, and a full payment postmarked or received by November 15 earns a 3% discount. You can also pay in thirds.

faqs.q: What is the Washington County real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: It is one dollar per thousand dollars of selling price, and buyer and seller share liability. You must pay it or file an exemption claim within 15 days of the recording date.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Washington County assessment?
faqs.a: File a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board between the date statements are mailed and December 31. There is no filing fee in Washington County, and the appeals line is 503-846-3854.

faqs.q: What does a yellow tax statement mean in Washington County?
faqs.a: A yellow statement means a mortgage company or the Oregon Department of Revenue requested the bill. If you recently bought, sold or refinanced, confirm with your lender that the tax will still be paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Washington County house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is normally paid from the proceeds through escrow, and the title company will order the figures. Foreclosure cannot start until three years after the earliest delinquency, so you generally have time to sell.
